requirement_results.command: restoring an item with no tombstone in the journal succeeds and is confirmed present on all 3 real backends
restoring a genuinely, independently-confirmed-deleted item is refused (REFUSED_TOMBSTONED) and the item remains absent from all 3 real backends afterward

a deletion saga that reports DELETION_INCOMPLETE (a target lies about tombstone success but the item is still findable) never tombstones the journal, so a later restore of a still-partially-present item is never wrongly refused
restore consults the tombstone journal before ever calling put()/contains()/tombstone() on any target -- proven directly via a call-order spy

a journal that cannot be reached (a real TCP connection refusal from a genuinely closed local port, not a simulated exception) is refused exactly like a tombstoned item (REFUSED_JOURNAL_UNAVAILABLE), never silently treated as safe to restore, and no target is touched
restoring a distinct, never-tombstoned item succeeds normally even immediately after an unrelated item's tombstone is recorded in the same journal
full local pytest regression, no new failures versus the pre-existing sandbox baseline (the two known interpreter-pin failures are unrelated and pre-existing)

residual_risks: The 'unreachable journal' fault-injection test uses a real OS-level TCP connection refusal (a DSN pointing at a genuinely closed local port) rather than pausing the shared ocor-bootstrap-postgresql-1 container: that container is used concurrently by many other sealed tasks' fixtures, and its CI provisioning is a native GitHub Actions services: block (not the docker run --name ocor-bootstrap-postgresql-1 convention fault_command() expects), so a real pause/unpause drill against it would require a broader, riskier CI refactor out of proportion to this task's specific acceptance criterion (the journal read path failing closed). The refusal exercised here is still a genuine network-layer fault, not a mocked exception.

record_deletion()/restore_from_backup() are a thin composition over the sealed OCOR-DEV-0025 saga and a new, minimal TombstoneJournal; no new DeletionTarget implementations were added -- PostgresMetadataTarget/TypeDBContentTarget/QdrantCacheTarget are reused byte-for-byte unmodified from spikes.memory_deletion.saga.

TombstoneJournal.ensure_schema() is deliberately separate from __init__ so that constructing a journal handle against a genuinely unreachable DSN (used by the fault-injection test) never itself raises before the read path under test runs; this is a spike-level convenience, not a claim about a hardened schema-migration story.
The same pre-existing local-venv gap noted in prior evidence (uv cannot resolve the exact 3.12.11 interpreter in this sandbox) is unchanged and out of this task's scope.
rollback_procedure_verified: Every test operates on a freshly generated, unique item_id (uuid4) and a fresh, self-provisioned Qdrant collection torn down in a finally block regardless of outcome, so no test leaves residual state another run could collide with. Verified directly by 4 consecutive full test-suite runs with no manual cleanup between them, and by the post-run stack-integrity check confirming all 11 persistent services remained healthy.
